opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I'd say first that I try to be careful not to over-read perplexity numbers. A better perplexity at a few hundred million or a billion-ish parameters doesn't, by itself, prove a whole paradigm. But I do think the results are meaningful evidence, for a specific reason.

The core claim of Nested Learning is that a model isn't one optimization problem with a fixed architecture sitting on top. It's a set of nested, interconnected optimization problems, each with its own context flow and its own update frequency. Attention, recurrent memory, even the optimizer itself can be seen as associative memory modules compressing their own context at different timescales. If that view is right, then the main bottleneck in current models is that they have basically two speeds: the weights, which are frozen after pre-training, and the context window, which is very fast but very short-lived. There's nothing in between.

Hope is our attempt to fill that gap directly. It builds on the Titans line of work, but adds two things. The first is self-modification, meaning the model learns how to update its own memory rather than relying on a fixed, hand-designed update rule. The second is what we call the continuum memory system, a spectrum of MLP blocks that update at different frequencies, so you get a gradient from fast to slow memory instead of just short-term and long-term.

So when Hope gets lower perplexity and better accuracy on common-sense reasoning benchmarks than strong baselines, including Transformers, modern recurrent models, and Titans itself, at matched scale, I read that as evidence that the extra levels are doing real work. The comparison to Titans matters most to me, because it's the closest ablation of the idea. The main thing we changed is adding more levels of learning and letting the model modify itself, and the language-modeling quality improved.

The other piece is that perplexity is fundamentally a measure of how well you compress and predict the stream you're seeing. Nested Learning is basically a theory about compression at multiple timescales. So it's natural that if you give the model a richer hierarchy of memories, each compressing its context at its own rate, you'd see it first in the most direct measure of predictive compression.

That said, I don't want to frame it as "perplexity went down, therefore the theory is proven." What I find more convincing is the pattern across results. You see gains in language modeling, in common-sense reasoning, and especially in long-context and needle-in-a-haystack-style tasks, where you'd expect multi-timescale memory to matter most. Taken together, that's consistent with the mechanism we hypothesized, not just a tuning win.

The open question, honestly, is scale. These experiments are at modest sizes, and the real test is whether the advantage holds or grows when you scale up. It also matters whether these levels let models do something closer to continual learning, actually absorbing new information after deployment rather than forgetting it once it leaves the context window. Perplexity is an early signal, but continual learning is the thing we really care about.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So first, I'd be careful about how much weight I put on the perplexity numbers by themselves, because Hope is really a proof of concept for the framework rather than the thing we're trying to sell. What we wanted to show is that if you take the Nested Learning view seriously, where you treat a model as a set of nested optimization problems, each with its own context flow and its own update frequency, you can actually derive an architecture from that, and the architecture should not fall apart. It should at least be competitive with the things people already use.

That's what the language modeling results are saying to me. We trained Hope at a few scales, something like 340 million up to 1.3 billion parameters, on the usual kind of data, and we compared it against Transformers, Titans, and the modern recurrent models like Mamba, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and so on. On perplexity, both on the held out language modeling sets and on the zero-shot commonsense reasoning tasks, Hope is either on par or a bit better than the baselines. So the first interpretation is simply: the design principles are not costing you anything. You get the self-modifying inner loop and the continuum memory system, and you don't pay for it in standard benchmarks.

The second thing, and this is the part I actually find more interesting, is where the gains show up. If you look at the long-context tasks, the needle-in-a-haystack style evaluations and the continual learning settings, the gap opens up. That's exactly where you would expect the Nested Learning story to matter, because that's where having memory modules that update at different time scales should help. A standard Transformer only has two levels, in-context learning in attention and the weights that are frozen after pre-training. Hope has multiple levels in between, with the continuum memory updating at intermediate frequencies, so it can consolidate information from the context into its parameters while it's running. So when we see the long-context improvements, I read that as evidence that the extra levels are doing real work, not just that we found a slightly better architecture by trial and error.

And the third thing is about the self-referential piece. In Hope, the model learns how to modify its own memory update rule, so it's not only learning from the data, it's learning its own learning algorithm in context. In the ablations, when we remove that, or when we flatten the memory hierarchy down to a single frequency, performance degrades, and it degrades most on the settings that require adapting to new distributions. So the perplexity results give you the sanity check, and the ablations plus the long-context and continual learning results give you the actual argument for the framework.

I should say, though, this is still early. These are not frontier scale models, and we haven't shown that the gains persist at tens or hundreds of billions of parameters. The honest claim is that Nested Learning gives you a principled way to design these systems, and Hope is one point in that design space that behaves the way the theory predicts. Whether it's the best point, I genuinely don't know yet.

astra-6.text:
I would interpret those results as evidence that Nested Learning can lead to useful architectural choices, rather than as proof of the whole framework. Perplexity asks a fairly specific question: how well does the model predict the next token? If Hope improves that under comparable training conditions, that suggests the design is helping it learn and use information more effectively.

The broader idea in Nested Learning is to think about learning as multiple interacting processes operating at different timescales. From that perspective, the interesting question is whether giving those processes a better structure translates into better language modeling. Hope’s results are encouraging in that sense.

But the comparison and the ablations matter. You want to distinguish the benefit of that structure from differences in parameter count, compute, or training setup. And lower perplexity alone doesn’t establish continual learning or show that a model can acquire new knowledge without forgetting. Those require direct tests. So I’d call the language-modeling results a useful validation of the approach, with a much broader set of claims still to investigate.

sol-6.1.text:
I would interpret them as evidence that Nested Learning can lead to a useful architecture, rather than as proof of the whole framework. Perplexity measures how well the model predicts the next token, so it gives us a concrete way to ask whether these ideas actually help with language modeling.

The key idea is that learning can happen at multiple levels, with different components updating at different timescales. Hope turns that perspective into a model. If that model achieves strong language-modeling performance, it suggests that organizing memory and learning this way is practically useful.

But the distinction is important: the result belongs to the particular architecture and training setup. To understand which parts support the broader Nested Learning argument, we need controlled comparisons and ablations. And perplexity alone doesn’t establish continual learning or the ability to retain knowledge over time. Those require their own evaluations. So I see these results as a promising demonstration of the framework’s usefulness, with more work needed to establish the full scope of its claims.
